title: One More Interview
focus: 确认问题、展示能力与说明限制
story:
Daniel offers me water before we sit down. Three people are waiting for me in the Northstar meeting room: Daniel, who leads project delivery, and two engineers, Mei and Omar.

I place my notebook on the table. I know Rui works somewhere in this building, but he is not part of my interview.

Daniel begins with a short description of the role. The team builds software for organisations with several locations. Developers work closely with the people who use the systems.

“You've worked mostly in a local team,” he says. “What would be new for you here?”

“Using English through the whole working day,” I say. “I can discuss technical work, but I sometimes need a question repeated. I haven't led regular client meetings in English.”

He nods. “Thank you for being clear.”

Then Mei asks about a project that had problems.

This time, I do not begin with the history of my old company.

“A report was too slow for daily use,” I say. “I measured where the time went and changed how we read the data. That helped, but it didn't solve everything.”

“What did you do next?”

“I showed the results to our manager. We released a smaller report first. I worked with another developer and a tester on the remaining parts.”

Omar asks what I would measure differently now. I need a moment, so I ask for one. Then I explain that I would test with more realistic amounts of data earlier.

Mei turns a sheet of paper toward me. It shows a small booking system. Two people are trying to reserve the same room.

“How would you handle a conflict?” she asks.

I almost begin talking about disagreements between colleagues. Then I look at the drawing.

“By conflict, do you mean two bookings for the same room and time?”

“Yes. Both people press confirm almost together.”

I draw two arrows and explain where I would check availability. Mei asks why checking only on the first screen is not enough.

“Because the room may become unavailable before the person confirms,” I say.

We discuss how to protect that final step. I forget a technical word halfway through an answer.

“I can't remember the English term,” I say. “I mean that these changes must succeed together, or none of them should remain.”

Omar supplies the word. I thank him and continue. The missing word does not end the discussion.

Near the end, Daniel asks if I have questions.

“What support is there for a developer who is new to client discussions?”

He explains that I would first join calls with him or another experienced colleague. I would still need to prepare, ask questions, and give updates. The job would not come with a personal English teacher.

“That sounds reasonable,” I say. “How do you share decisions after a call?”

“We write them down. Sometimes we need a reminder to do it.”

He smiles briefly, then checks the time. Our hour is finished.

I leave tired, with no idea what their decision will be. On the metro, I write down one question I answered badly. Then I write down one I clarified before answering.

Over the next two weeks, I complete the remaining recruitment steps. I have a final conversation with the hiring team and give permission for them to contact my references. Waiting still makes it difficult to sleep some nights.

The offer arrives on a Monday afternoon. I read the role, pay, and conditions slowly. Then I speak with the recruiter to check the details before accepting. My start date is three weeks away.

When Maya comes home, I am setting two plates on the table.

“I have news,” I say.

She puts down her bag. “Good news?”

“Yes. Northstar offered me the job. I accepted.”

She grins and pulls out her chair. “Tell me.”

I tell her about the money and the start date. She asks if I am pleased. It takes me a moment to say yes. For weeks, every time I open my mouth to talk about work, I have to explain what happened to my old team. I still have the start of that sentence ready.

“Did you show yours today?” I ask. There is blue tape on the sleeve of her coat. She takes it off and rolls it between her fingers.

“Both versions. They chose the safe one.”

“Which one is that?”

“The one they've already seen about twelve times.”

I get up to fetch the food. From beside the stove I ask, “Could you show the other one to—”

“Andy, I spent the afternoon hearing what I could do.”

I turn the heat down and bring the pan to the table. “What happened when you showed them yours?”

She makes a place for the pan. “Somebody at the back moved his chair closer. I thought he wanted to see my drawing. He wanted to plug in his computer.” She gives a small laugh. “But the woman beside him asked where I got the idea. I did get to answer that.”

She tells me about a morning spent watching people try to read a sign from the end of a hall. She gets up halfway through dinner to show me how far away they stood. Her version has fewer words; you can read them without walking all the way to the wall.

“Like your print in the kitchen,” I say.

“Yes. Exactly like that.”

When we finally eat, the rice at the bottom of the pan is brown. We both like that part. Maya divides it with the edge of the spoon, very carefully, as if there might be a serious argument about who gets more.

“Three weeks,” she says, passing me my share. “You'll have to start getting up before me again.”

I had forgotten that part of having a job.

phrases.en: What would be new for you?
phrases.zh: 询问可能面临的新挑战

phrases.en: I sometimes need a question repeated.
I need a moment to think.
How do you share decisions after a call?

practice.grammar: 用 would 描述假设情境中的做法：I would check availability again before confirming. 把 would 后面的动词保持原形，再补充具体条件。
practice.pronunciation: 朗读 By conflict, / do you mean TWO bookings / for the SAME room and time? 在关键词前后留小停顿，强调 two 与 same；再换一个工作关键词练习。

questions.q: What does Andy clarify before answering Mei's question?
questions.a: He checks that conflict means two bookings for the same room and time.

questions.q: Which version does Maya's client choose?
questions.a: The client chooses the familiar version instead of Maya's own design.

questions.q: When will Andy start at Northstar?
questions.a: He will start three weeks after accepting the offer.

roleplay.context: 你扮演 Andy，参加一个讨论预订系统的技术面试。

turns.line: How would you handle a conflict?
turns.cue: 先确认 conflict 是指重复预订还是团队意见不一致。

turns.line: Two people want the same room at the same time.
turns.cue: 说明检查步骤和你这样做的原因。

turns.line: Do you have any questions for us?
turns.cue: 询问新员工参与客户沟通时能获得的支持。

practice.transfer: 换到跨团队会议：对方说 We need better performance。先口头确认 performance 指速度、稳定性还是其他指标，再提出一个你能检查的具体项目。
practice.retell: 用一至两分钟复述面试：坦诚说明限制、讲项目、确认歧义、解释忘记的术语、询问支持，以及完成流程后的结果。不要把获得工作说成英语已完美。

translations.12-1: 入座前，Daniel 先问我要不要喝水。
translations.12-2: Northstar 的会议室里有三个人在等我：负责项目交付的 Daniel，以及两位工程师 Mei 和 Omar。
translations.12-4: 我知道 Rui 就在这栋楼的某个地方工作，但他不参与我的面试。
translations.12-5: Daniel 先简单介绍了这个岗位。
translations.12-6: 团队为设有多个地点的机构开发软件。
translations.12-7: 开发人员会和系统的使用者密切合作。
translations.12-8: “你过去主要在本地团队工作，”他说。
translations.12-9: “这里有哪些方面对你来说会是新的？”
translations.12-11: “我能讨论技术工作，不过有时需要别人把问题再说一遍。
translations.12-12: 我还没有定期用英语主持过客户会议。”
translations.12-15: 接着，Mei 问起一个遇到过问题的项目。
translations.12-16: 这一次，我没有从老公司的历史讲起。
translations.12-17: “一份报表运行太慢，没法满足日常使用，”我说。
translations.12-18: “我测了时间花在哪里，然后调整了读取数据的方式。
translations.12-19: 这样有帮助，但没能解决所有问题。”
translations.12-22: 我们先发布了一个精简版报表。
translations.12-23: 剩下的部分，我和另一位开发人员、一位测试人员一起完成。”
translations.12-24: Omar 问我，如果现在来做，我会在哪些测量上采取不同做法。
translations.12-25: 我需要一点时间想想，就直接提了出来。
translations.12-26: 然后我解释，我会更早用贴近实际的数据量进行测试。
translations.12-28: 上面画着一个小型预订系统。
translations.12-29: 两个人正试着预订同一间会议室。
translations.12-31: 我差点开始讲如何处理同事之间的分歧。
translations.12-33: “您说的冲突，是指两笔预订选了同一个房间、同一个时间吗？”
translations.12-35: 两个人几乎同时点击确认。”
translations.12-36: 我画了两个箭头，解释我会在哪一步检查是否可预订。
translations.12-37: Mei 问，为什么只在第一个页面检查还不够。
translations.12-38: “因为在用户确认之前，这间房可能已经被订走了，”我说。
translations.12-39: 我们讨论了如何保障最后这一步。
translations.12-40: 回答到一半，我忘了一个技术术语。
translations.12-41: “我想不起那个英文术语了，”我说。
translations.12-42: “我的意思是，这些修改要么一起成功，要么一项也不能保留。”
translations.12-43: Omar 帮我说出了那个词。
translations.12-45: 忘了一个词，并没有让讨论就此结束。
translations.12-46: 快结束时，Daniel 问我有没有问题。
translations.12-47: “对于刚开始参与客户讨论的开发人员，公司会提供什么支持？”
translations.12-48: 他解释，一开始我会和他或其他有经验的同事一起参加通话。
translations.12-49: 我仍然需要准备、提问，并汇报进展。
translations.12-50: 这份工作不会附带一位私人英语老师。
translations.12-52: “通话之后，你们怎么同步做出的决定？”
translations.12-54: 有时候也需要有人提醒才会记。”
translations.12-55: 他短暂地笑了一下，然后看了看时间。
translations.12-57: 离开时，我很疲惫，也完全不知道他们会做出什么决定。
translations.12-58: 在地铁上，我记下一道答得不好的问题。
translations.12-59: 然后又记下一道我在回答前先确认过的问题。
translations.12-60: 接下来的两周里，我完成了剩余的招聘流程。
translations.12-61: 我和招聘团队做了最后一次沟通，并同意他们联系我的推荐人。
translations.12-62: 等待仍让我有几个晚上难以入睡。
translations.12-63: 录用通知在一个周一下午发来了。
translations.12-64: 我慢慢读完岗位、薪酬和各项条件。
translations.12-65: 随后，我跟招聘人员通话核实细节，再接受了邀请。
translations.12-67: Maya 回家时，我正在桌上摆两只盘子。
translations.12-72: Northstar 给我发了录用通知。
translations.12-76: 我把工资和入职日期都告诉了她。
translations.12-78: 我过了一会儿才说，开心。
translations.12-79: 这些个星期，每次开口聊到工作，我总得先解释以前的团队出了什么事。
translations.12-80: 那句解释的开头还在我嘴边。
translations.12-81: “今天你把自己的设计给他们看了吗？”我问。
translations.12-82: 她外套的袖子上粘着一段蓝胶带。
translations.12-83: 她揭下来，在指间搓成一卷。
translations.12-85: 他们选了最稳妥的那版。”
translations.12-87: “就是他们已经看过十来遍的那版。”
translations.12-89: 我站在炉边问：“你能不能把另一版给——”
translations.12-90: “Andy，整个下午我都在听别人说我可以怎么做。”
translations.12-91: 我把火调小，端着锅走到桌边。
translations.12-92: “你把自己的那版给他们看的时候，怎么样？”
translations.12-94: “后面有个人把椅子往前挪了挪。
translations.12-95: 我还以为他想看我的画。
translations.12-98: “不过，他旁边那位女士问我的想法是从哪儿来的。
translations.12-99: 这件事我倒真有机会讲了。”
translations.12-100: 她说有天早上，她一直在看人们怎样站在大厅尽头辨认一块指示牌。
translations.12-101: 饭吃到一半，她还站起来，比给我看那些人当时站得有多远。
translations.12-102: 她那版字少些，不用一直走到墙边就能读清。
translations.12-103: “就像你放在厨房的那张样稿，”我说。
translations.12-106: 等我们总算开始好好吃饭，锅底的米已经焦黄了。
translations.12-108: Maya 小心翼翼地用勺子边把它分开，好像谁多分一点，我们就真会吵起来似的。
translations.12-109: “三个星期，”她把我那份递过来说。
translations.12-110: “到时候你又得比我先起床了。”
translations.12-111: 我都忘了上班还有这么一回事。
